items.group_name: Use of data and information
items.blueprint: AUD.III.A Use of data and information [III.A.2]
items.topic: Reliability of a system-generated report
items.task: Request, prepare and assess the reliability of data and information used in an engagement.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Riverbend Wholesale, a nonissuer, receives a system-generated accounts receivable aging report and plans to use it to select balances for confirmation. Which procedure best addresses the reliability of the report before it is used?
options: Reconcile its total to the general ledger and test the controls over its preparation, to establish accuracy and completeness
Ask management to certify in writing that the report is accurate and use it without further procedures
Rely on the report because it was produced by the entity's accounting system rather than being prepared manually by a person
Test only the ten largest balances on the report for existence
items.rule_line: Evaluate the accuracy and completeness of information the entity produces before using it as audit evidence.

why.A: Correct. The auditor evaluates whether information is accurate and complete, for example by reconciling it and testing controls over its preparation.
why.B: A representation is not a substitute for evidence about the accuracy and completeness of the information.
why.C: System output can be inaccurate or incomplete, and favoring automated output without evaluation is a bias.
why.D: Testing existence of the largest balances says nothing about whether the report is complete.

guide.ask: What must the auditor establish about a system-generated report before using it?
guide.reveal: That it is accurate and complete.

guide.ask: Which procedure does that?
guide.reveal: Reconciling its total to the general ledger and testing controls over its preparation.

items.group_name: Use of data and information
items.blueprint: AUD.III.A Use of data and information [III.A.1]
items.topic: Completeness of an extracted data population
items.task: Request, prepare and transform data for use in an engagement.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Summit Rail, a nonissuer, asks the IT department for an extract of all 2025 purchase transactions to test for duplicate payments with data analytics. Which step most directly supports the completeness of the extracted population?
options: Obtain an email from the IT department stating that the extract includes all transactions
Sort the extract by vendor name and remove rows with missing vendor numbers before running the analytics
Select a sample of vendors from the extract and confirm that they exist
Reconcile the record count and control totals of the extract to the general ledger and subledger totals
items.rule_line: Reconcile extracted data to the accounting records to establish completeness before running analytics.

why.A: An assertion from IT is not evidence about completeness of the extract.
why.B: Removing rows before analysis can make the population less complete, not more.
why.C: Confirming existence of vendors addresses validity, not whether all transactions were extracted.
why.D: Correct. Reconciling counts and totals to the accounting records tests whether the population is complete.

guide.ask: What does completeness of an extract mean?
guide.reveal: All transactions in the period are included.

guide.ask: Which step tests that against independent records?
guide.reveal: Reconciling record counts and control totals to the ledger and subledger.

items.group_name: Use of data and information
items.blueprint: AUD.III.A Use of data and information [III.A.3]
items.topic: Using data analytics results
items.task: Use the outputs of data analytic techniques to assist in risk assessment or to complete planned procedures.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Using an analytics tool, the auditor of Coral Bay Resorts, a nonissuer, isolates 412 of 38,000 journal entries that were posted on weekends by users with no accounting role. Which use of the results is most appropriate?
options: Conclude that the 38,000 unflagged entries are appropriate because the tool examined the entire population
Treat all 412 flagged entries as errors and propose adjustments for each one
Select 25 of the 412 at random and project the results to all 38,000 entries
Investigate the flagged entries for purpose and authorization, and use the results in assessing override risk
items.rule_line: Analytics flags items for investigation; the auditor evaluates the flagged items and does not treat the unflagged population as cleared.

why.A: The tool applied specific criteria; entries that pass those criteria are not shown to be appropriate.
why.B: Flagged entries are unusual, not necessarily wrong, so the auditor investigates before concluding.
why.C: Results from the flagged group cannot be projected to a population that was not sampled from.
why.D: Correct. Flagged entries call for investigation of purpose and authorization, and the results inform the override risk assessment.

guide.ask: What do the flagged weekend entries by non-accounting users suggest?
guide.reveal: Possible unauthorized or unusual postings that need follow-up.

guide.ask: How should the auditor use them?
guide.reveal: Investigate purpose and authorization and use the results in assessing management override risk.

items.group_name: Use of data and information
items.blueprint: AUD.III.A Use of data and information [III.A.2]
items.topic: Attributes affecting reliability of information
items.task: Assess the reliability of data and information.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which set of attributes affects the reliability of information used as audit evidence under AICPA standards?
options: Materiality, timeliness, cost and convenience of obtaining the information in question
Accuracy, completeness, authenticity and susceptibility to management bias
Persuasiveness, sufficiency, precision and volume
Size, format, storage location and age of the record
items.rule_line: Reliability depends on accuracy, completeness, authenticity and susceptibility to management bias.

why.A: Cost and convenience are not attributes of reliability.
why.B: Correct. Reliability is affected, to varying degrees, by accuracy, completeness, authenticity and susceptibility to management bias.
why.C: Sufficiency concerns the quantity of evidence rather than the reliability of information.
why.D: Format and location may matter for procedures but are not the listed attributes.

guide.ask: Which attributes affect reliability of information used as evidence?
guide.reveal: Whether it is accurate, complete and authentic, and whether it can be biased by management.

guide.ask: Which list matches?
guide.reveal: Accuracy, completeness, authenticity and susceptibility to bias.

items.group_name: Sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.B Sufficient appropriate evidence [III.B]
items.topic: Relative reliability of evidence
items.task: Identify sources of evidence and conclude on whether evidence obtained achieves the engagement's objectives.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In auditing the existence of cash at Ardent Fabrics, a nonissuer, the auditor considers four sources of evidence. Which is most reliable?
options: A bank confirmation the auditor receives directly from the bank
A bank statement retained in the treasurer's files and provided to the auditor
Management's oral explanation of the year-end cash position
A photocopy of a bank reconciliation prepared by client staff
items.rule_line: Reliability is higher for external sources, direct acquisition by the auditor, and documentary forms.

why.A: Correct. Evidence from an external party obtained directly by the auditor is generally the most reliable.
why.B: A document retained by the client and provided by management is internal and obtained indirectly.
why.C: Oral representations are generally less reliable than documentary evidence.
why.D: A client-prepared reconciliation is internal evidence, and a photocopy is less reliable than an original.

guide.ask: What generally makes evidence more reliable?
guide.reveal: Coming from an independent external source directly to the auditor.

guide.ask: Which source fits?
guide.reveal: The bank confirmation received directly from the bank.

items.group_name: Sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.B Sufficient appropriate evidence [III.B]
items.topic: Sufficiency and appropriateness
items.task: Conclude on whether evidence obtained achieves the engagement's planned objectives.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the sufficiency and appropriateness of audit evidence?
options: Sufficiency measures the reliability of evidence, and appropriateness measures the number of items tested.
Sufficiency and appropriateness are the same measure of evidence, described with different terms by different standards.
Sufficiency measures quantity of evidence, and appropriateness measures its quality, including relevance and reliability.
A larger quantity of evidence can compensate for evidence of poor quality, provided the total is substantial.
items.rule_line: Sufficiency is quantity; appropriateness is quality (relevance and reliability).

why.A: The definitions are reversed.
why.B: They are distinct: one is quantity and the other is quality.
why.C: Correct. Sufficiency concerns quantity and appropriateness concerns quality, which includes relevance and reliability.
why.D: Quantity does not make up for poor quality; the amount needed depends on risk and the quality of the evidence.

verify.note: AS 1105.05-.06 원문 확인, AU-C 500.05 도 동일(충분성=양, 적합성=질). 정답 C 유효.

guide.ask: What does sufficiency measure?
guide.reveal: The quantity of evidence.

guide.ask: What does appropriateness measure?
guide.reveal: Its quality, meaning relevance and reliability; more quantity cannot make up for poor quality.

items.group_name: Sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.B Sufficient appropriate evidence [III.B]
items.topic: Inconsistent audit evidence
items.task: Conclude on whether evidence obtained achieves the engagement's planned objectives.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Marsh Energy, a nonissuer, receives a supplier confirmation showing a payable of $420,000, while the company's accounts payable subledger shows $310,000. Management says the difference is due to an invoice that has not been recorded yet. What should the auditor do?
options: Determine whether modified or additional procedures are needed to resolve the difference, such as examining the unrecorded invoice
Accept the subledger balance, because management knows the supplier relationship and the timing of its invoices better than the supplier's confirmation shows
Average the confirmed and recorded amounts to estimate the payable
Disregard the confirmation, because it conflicts with the entity's own records
items.rule_line: Resolve inconsistencies in audit evidence with modified or additional procedures.

why.A: Correct. Inconsistent evidence from two sources requires the auditor to determine what modified or additional procedures will resolve it.
why.B: Management's explanation is uncorroborated and cannot outweigh contradictory evidence from an external party.
why.C: Averaging does not resolve the difference or determine which amount is right.
why.D: Contradictory external evidence cannot be disregarded because it disagrees with internal records; it points to possible unrecorded liabilities.

guide.ask: What do the two sources say, and do they agree?
guide.reveal: Confirmation shows $420,000 and the subledger $310,000, a $110,000 difference.

guide.ask: How should the auditor treat management's explanation?
guide.reveal: Determine what modified or additional procedures are needed to resolve it, such as examining the unrecorded invoice.

items.group_name: Sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.B Sufficient appropriate evidence [III.B]
items.topic: Using company-produced information in an issuer audit
items.task: Assess the reliability of data and information used as evidence.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: An auditor of an issuer plans to use a company-produced inventory listing as audit evidence. What do PCAOB standards require the auditor to do?
options: Test the completeness of the listing only, because accuracy is presumed for electronically produced company data
Nothing further, provided the listing was produced by the company's ERP system and reconciles to the general ledger total
Obtain a written management representation about the accuracy of the listing and the completeness of the items on it
Test the accuracy and completeness of the information, or the controls over them, and evaluate its precision and detail
items.rule_line: For company-produced information, test accuracy and completeness (or controls over them) and evaluate precision.

why.A: Both accuracy and completeness must be addressed.
why.B: System production does not remove the requirement to evaluate the information.
why.C: A representation does not replace testing accuracy and completeness or the controls over them.
why.D: Correct. The auditor must test accuracy and completeness, or the controls over them, and evaluate whether the information is sufficiently precise and detailed.

guide.ask: What must be evaluated for company-produced information?
guide.reveal: Accuracy and completeness of the information.

guide.ask: What does the PCAOB add?
guide.reveal: Test those or the controls over them, and evaluate whether it is precise and detailed enough.

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Factors affecting sample size for a test of controls
items.task: Determine appropriate populations and sample size for sampling.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: An auditor designs a test of controls over credit approvals at Fenwick Retail, a nonissuer. Holding other factors constant, which change would increase the required sample size?
options: A higher acceptable risk of overreliance
A decrease in the tolerable rate of deviation
A decrease in the expected rate of deviation
An increase in the tolerable rate of deviation
items.rule_line: Sample size rises as the tolerable deviation rate falls, the expected deviation rate rises, or the desired assurance rises.

why.A: Accepting a higher risk of overreliance means less assurance is needed, so the sample can be smaller.
why.B: Correct. A lower tolerable rate of deviation requires more evidence and a larger sample.
why.C: A lower expected deviation rate reduces the sample size.
why.D: A higher tolerable rate requires less precision, so the sample can be smaller.

guide.ask: What does a lower tolerable deviation rate demand?
guide.reveal: More precise evidence.

guide.ask: Which change raises sample size?
guide.reveal: A decrease in the tolerable rate of deviation.

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Evaluating a test of controls sample
items.task: Evaluate results of sampling procedures for tests of controls.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Larkin Distributors, a nonissuer, tests 80 sales invoices for evidence of credit approval and finds no approval on 6 of them. The tolerable rate of deviation is 5%, and the expected rate was 1%. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The sample deviation rate is 7.5%, but no conclusion about reliance is possible without a statistical projection to the population.
The sample deviation rate is 1.3%, which is below the tolerable rate, so the planned reliance on the control is supported.
The sample deviation rate is 7.5%, which exceeds the tolerable rate, so the planned reliance on the control is not supported.
The sample deviation rate is 6.0%, which exceeds the tolerable rate, so the planned reliance on the control is not supported.
items.rule_line: For a test of controls, the sample deviation rate is the projected rate and is compared with the tolerable rate.

why.A: For tests of controls, the sample deviation rate is the projected deviation rate for the population.
why.B: This divides by the wrong base and also ignores that 6 deviations were found, not 1.
why.C: Correct. 6 / 80 = 7.5%, and for tests of controls the sample deviation rate is also the projected rate, which exceeds the 5% tolerable rate.
why.D: The rate is computed on 80 items, not 100; 6 / 100 would give 6.0% but the sample is 80.

steps: 7.5% > tolerable rate 5%, so reliance is not supported

guide.ask: What is the sample deviation rate?
Compare with the tolerable rate.
guide.reveal: It exceeds 5%, and in a test of controls the sample rate is the projected rate, so planned reliance is not supported.

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Projecting a misstatement found in a sample
items.task: Project the results of sampling and extrapolate misstatements.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Larkin Distributors, a nonissuer, tests accounts receivable using a nonstatistical sample. The population has 1,500 accounts with a recorded amount of $3,000,000. The sample has 100 accounts with a recorded amount of $210,000, and the auditor finds overstatements of $8,400 in the sample. Using the ratio of sample misstatement to sample recorded amount, what is the projected misstatement for the population?
items.rule_line: Ratio projection multiplies the population's recorded amount by the ratio of sample misstatement to sample recorded amount.

why.A: This is the misstatement found in the sample, not projected to the population.
why.B: This multiplies the sample misstatement by 10, which has no basis in the population-to-sample relationship.
why.D: This projects the average misstatement per item ($84) over 1,500 accounts, a different method (difference estimation).

guide.ask: What is the ratio of misstatement to recorded amount in the sample?
Apply it to the population.

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Sampling risk when projected misstatement is near tolerable
items.task: Evaluate the results of sampling, including sampling risk.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In the receivables test of Larkin Distributors, a nonissuer, the projected misstatement is $120,000 and tolerable misstatement is $130,000. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The misstatements found in the sample can be ignored, because the sample is small relative to the population
The balance is not materially misstated because $120,000 is below the tolerable misstatement of $130,000, so no further work is needed
The auditor should record $120,000 as an audit adjustment, because a projection is the best measure of the actual misstatement in the balance
Sampling risk is significant because the projection is close to tolerable misstatement; consider extending testing or asking management to adjust
items.rule_line: A projected misstatement near tolerable misstatement signals unacceptable sampling risk.

why.A: Misstatements identified in a sample must be investigated, projected and evaluated.
why.B: A projection below tolerable misstatement does not by itself give assurance when it is close, because of sampling risk.
why.C: Due to sampling risk, a projection may not be sufficient to determine an amount to be recorded.
why.D: Correct. When projected misstatement is close to tolerable misstatement, the risk that actual misstatement exceeds it is unacceptable, so more work or correction is considered.
