guide.ask: How close is the projection to tolerable misstatement?
What does that closeness suggest?
guide.reveal: A significant chance the true misstatement exceeds the tolerable amount, so consider extending testing or asking for an adjustment.

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Monetary-unit sample size
items.task: Determine sample size for a substantive test using monetary-unit sampling.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Brookline Marine, a nonissuer, uses monetary-unit sampling for a receivables population of $2,400,000. Tolerable misstatement is $80,000, the auditor expects no misstatements, and the reliability factor for the desired risk of incorrect acceptance is 3.0. What sample size results, using population divided by the sampling interval, where the interval equals tolerable misstatement divided by the reliability factor?
items.rule_line: Monetary-unit sample size equals the population divided by the sampling interval, where interval is tolerable misstatement divided by the reliability factor.

why.A: This divides the population by tolerable misstatement and omits the reliability factor.
why.B: This uses a tolerable misstatement of $100,000 rather than $80,000.
why.D: This is the sampling interval in dollars, not the number of items in the sample.

cite.ref: Audit Sampling audit guide (formula; guide text not opened)

guide.ask: How is the sampling interval found?
guide.reveal: Tolerable misstatement over the reliability factor: $80,000 / 3.0 = $26,667.

guide.ask: Then the sample size?

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Statistical versus nonstatistical sampling
items.task: Understand sampling techniques, including statistical and nonstatistical approaches.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which characteristics make a sampling approach statistical under AICPA standards?
options: Selection of items that the auditor judges to be representative of the population being tested
Random selection of items plus a statistical technique to evaluate results, including sampling risk
Use of computer software to select the sample items from the population without manual intervention
A sample size that is large enough, such as more than 100 items drawn from the population under test
items.rule_line: Statistical sampling combines random selection with a statistical technique for evaluating results.

why.A: Judgmental selection is nonstatistical because it lacks random selection.
why.B: Correct. Statistical sampling requires random selection and statistical evaluation of results, including measurement of sampling risk.
why.C: Software can select items in a nonstatistical way; the definition is about random selection and statistical evaluation.
why.D: Sample size is not a valid criterion for choosing between statistical and nonstatistical approaches.

guide.ask: What two features define statistical sampling?
guide.reveal: Random selection and a statistical way of evaluating results.

guide.ask: Which choice states them?
guide.reveal: The one requiring random selection and statistical evaluation including sampling risk; software use and size alone do not qualify.

items.group_name: Sampling techniques
items.blueprint: AUD.III.C Sampling techniques [III.C]
items.topic: Stratifying a population
items.task: Apply stratification and determine appropriate populations for sampling.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Oakmont Supply, a nonissuer, has 1,940 receivable balances. Forty balances over $100,000 make up 55% of the total dollar amount, and the rest are small. The auditor wants an efficient and effective substantive test. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Examine the 40 large balances separately and select a sample from the remaining small balances
Take a random sample of 60 from the entire population and give the large balances no separate consideration
Select the sample only from the 40 large balances and extrapolate the results to all 1,940
Take a haphazard sample of 60 items from the whole population without regard to size
items.rule_line: Examine high-value items separately, stratify the population, and sample the remainder.

why.A: Correct. Items of high value or risk can be examined separately and sampling applied to the rest, or the population can be stratified.
why.B: A simple random sample could miss most large items, so it may not be an effective response.
why.C: Results from the large balances cannot be projected to the small balances that were not sampled.
why.D: A sample that ignores size may miss most of the dollars in the large balances.

guide.ask: Do 40 balances covering over half the dollars deserve separate attention?
guide.reveal: Yes, they carry high value.

guide.ask: What is the efficient design?
guide.reveal: Examine the large items separately and sample from the remaining small balances.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.1]
items.topic: Tests of controls over time
items.task: Use observation and inspection to test controls.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Foxglove Pharma, a nonissuer, plans to rely on a control requiring supervisor approval of purchase orders above $10,000. Which procedure provides the most persuasive evidence of operating effectiveness throughout the period?
options: Inquire of the purchasing manager about how approvals of purchase orders over $10,000 are performed
Observe a supervisor approving purchase orders on one day during fieldwork
Inspect a sample of purchase orders from throughout the year for evidence of supervisor approval
Read the purchasing policy manual that requires supervisor approval
items.rule_line: Tests of controls combine inquiry with inspection, observation or reperformance across the period.

why.A: Inquiry alone does not provide sufficient evidence of operating effectiveness.
why.B: Observation covers only the time it is performed and does not show the control operated all year.
why.C: Correct. Inspecting items from across the period gives evidence of how the control was applied and its consistency, beyond inquiry alone.
why.D: A policy manual shows what should happen, not that it did happen.

guide.ask: Which procedures give evidence over the whole period?
guide.reveal: Those applied to items across the period, beyond inquiry, observation on one day or reading a policy.

guide.ask: Which choice does that?
guide.reveal: Inspecting a sample of purchase orders from throughout the year for approval.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.1]
items.topic: Extending interim control testing to year-end
items.task: Use tests of controls to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Halden Furniture, a nonissuer with a December 31 year-end, tested a control over sales returns approvals at October 31 and found it effective. The auditor plans to rely on the control for the full year. What is required?
options: Retest the control for the entire year, because interim evidence has no value
Obtain evidence on changes to the control after October 31 and decide what added evidence the remaining period needs
Obtain a management representation that the control operated as designed until year-end
Nothing further, because a control that was effective at interim is assumed to keep operating effectively until year-end
items.rule_line: Interim control test results are extended to year-end through evidence of changes and procedures for the remaining period.

why.A: Interim evidence can be used with additional evidence for the remaining period; retesting the whole year is not required.
why.B: Correct. When interim evidence is used, the auditor obtains evidence about significant changes and determines additional evidence for the remaining period.
why.C: A representation is not sufficient evidence about operating effectiveness.
why.D: Effectiveness at interim does not establish effectiveness for the remaining period.

guide.ask: What does interim testing cover and what does it leave?
guide.reveal: It covers the period to October 31, but not November and December.

guide.ask: What must the auditor obtain?
guide.reveal: Evidence about changes after the interim date and decide what additional evidence the remaining period needs.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.1]
items.topic: Relying on prior-year control testing
items.task: Use tests of controls to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Kingfisher Cabinets, a nonissuer, tested an automated control over inventory costing in the 2023 audit with no exceptions. In 2024 the auditor used the 2023 evidence, performing inquiry with observation to confirm no changes. For 2025 the auditor wants to use the 2023 evidence again. Which statement is correct?
options: The control must be tested in the 2025 audit, because controls must be tested at least once in every third audit
The auditor must test every control the auditor relies on in every audit, without exception
The 2023 evidence can be used again in 2025 if there were no changes, because retesting is required only every fifth audit
The 2023 evidence can be used again in 2025 if the auditor makes inquiries of management only
items.rule_line: Prior-audit control evidence may be used if still relevant, but controls must be tested at least once every third audit.

why.A: Correct. If evidence from a previous audit is used and there have been no changes, the control is tested at least once in every third audit. The 2023 test means 2025 is the third audit.
why.B: The standard allows use of prior evidence, subject to the every-third-audit limit and other conditions.
why.C: The interval is every third audit, not every fifth.
why.D: Continuing relevance requires inquiry combined with observation or inspection, and testing at least every third audit; inquiry alone is not enough.

guide.ask: How often must a relied-upon control be tested when earlier evidence is reused and nothing changes?
guide.reveal: At least once in every third audit.

guide.ask: Count from 2023.
guide.reveal: 2023 was the first, 2024 the second, so 2025 is the third and requires testing.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.2]
items.topic: Requirements for substantive analytical procedures
items.task: Perform analytical procedures to obtain evidence.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which of the following is required when an auditor designs substantive analytical procedures for a nonissuer audit?
options: Use the recorded amounts as the basis for the expectation, so that the comparison is consistent
Investigate every difference regardless of amount, since any difference may indicate a misstatement
Perform the procedure only after completing tests of details on the same assertion so results can be compared
Develop a precise expectation and determine the difference that is acceptable without further investigation
items.rule_line: Substantive analytics require a precise expectation, reliable data, and a preset acceptable difference.

why.A: An expectation based on the recorded amounts is not independent and would not detect misstatements.
why.B: The auditor investigates differences that exceed the acceptable amount; investigation of every difference is not required.
why.C: Analytical procedures may be performed alone or with tests of details.
why.D: Correct. The auditor develops a sufficiently precise expectation and determines the acceptable difference before comparing recorded amounts.

guide.ask: What must be done before comparing recorded amounts in a substantive analytic?
guide.reveal: Build an expectation that is precise enough to be useful.

guide.ask: What else is set in advance?
guide.reveal: The difference that is acceptable without further investigation.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.2]
items.topic: Investigating an analytical difference
items.task: Recalculate and evaluate analytical procedure results.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Tanager Foods, a nonissuer, had 240 average employees in 2025 at an average salary of $52,000. Recorded wages are $13,080,000. The auditor's expectation is number of employees times average salary, and the auditor will investigate differences above $400,000. What is the appropriate action?
options: Investigate the $600,000 difference by inquiry and corroboration, because it exceeds the $400,000 threshold
Raise the threshold to $600,000 so that the difference does not require investigation or documentation
Take no further action, because the difference is under 5% of the recorded wages for the year
Reduce recorded wages by $600,000 to agree to the expectation
items.rule_line: Investigate differences from expectation that exceed the predetermined acceptable amount.

why.A: Correct. Expected wages are 240 x $52,000 = $12,480,000. The difference of $600,000 exceeds the threshold, so it must be investigated.
why.B: Changing the threshold after seeing the difference would defeat the purpose of setting it in advance.
why.C: The threshold is the auditor's predetermined amount of $400,000; the difference is 4.6% of recorded wages, but percentage is not the criterion.
why.D: The expectation is an estimate used to evaluate the recorded amount, not a basis for adjusting it.

guide.ask: What is the expectation for wages?
Compare the difference with the threshold.
guide.reveal: $13,080,000 - $12,480,000 = $600,000, above $400,000, so investigate by inquiry and corroboration.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.2]
items.topic: Analytical procedures near the end of the audit
items.task: Perform analytical procedures to obtain evidence.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Near the end of the 2025 audit of Tanager Foods, a nonissuer, the auditor performs analytical procedures on the financial statements as a whole. What is their purpose?
options: To replace substantive procedures for accounts that the auditor has assessed as low risk of material misstatement
To help form an overall conclusion about consistency with the auditor's understanding of the entity
To determine the level of materiality for the financial statements as a whole
To identify whether individual transactions were recorded in the wrong period
items.rule_line: End-of-audit analytical procedures support the auditor's overall conclusion on the financial statements.

why.A: Overall analytics do not replace substantive procedures.
why.B: Correct. Analytical procedures near the end of the audit help form an overall conclusion about consistency with the auditor's understanding.
why.C: Materiality is determined during planning and revised as the audit progresses, not by these procedures.
why.D: Testing individual transactions for cutoff is done through detailed procedures.

guide.ask: When are analytics performed on the statements as a whole?
guide.reveal: Near the end of the audit.

guide.ask: What is their purpose then?
guide.reveal: To form an overall conclusion about consistency with the auditor's understanding of the entity.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.2]
items.topic: Reliability of data used in analytics
items.task: Assess the reliability of data used in analytical procedures.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Elmwood Hospitality, a nonissuer, plans a substantive analytical procedure on utilities expense using square footage data maintained by facilities staff in an unreviewed spreadsheet. No controls over the spreadsheet have been evaluated. What should the auditor do?
options: Use prior-year utilities expense as the expectation and treat the absence of a difference as sufficient
Widen the acceptable difference to allow for possible errors in the spreadsheet
Proceed with the analytics as planned, because analytical procedures are generally less sensitive to data quality than tests of details are
Evaluate the reliability of the data, including controls over its preparation, and obtain more evidence or change the procedure
items.rule_line: Evaluate the reliability of data used to develop an analytical expectation.

why.A: Prior-year expense as expectation ignores changes and does not address the data problem.
why.B: Widening the threshold reduces the procedure's ability to detect misstatements rather than addressing reliability.
why.C: An expectation is only as good as its underlying data, so data quality matters for analytics.
why.D: Correct. The auditor evaluates the reliability of the data behind the expectation and obtains further evidence or changes the procedure if it is not reliable.

guide.ask: What is the weakness in the expectation's data?
guide.reveal: An unreviewed spreadsheet with no evaluated controls.

guide.ask: What must the auditor do?
guide.reveal: Evaluate the reliability of the data and its controls, and get more evidence or change the procedure.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.3]
items.topic: Negative confirmation requirements
items.task: Perform external confirmations.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Westfield Water Utility, a nonissuer, wants to use negative confirmations as the sole substantive procedure for 30,000 small residential receivable balances. Which condition must be present?
options: The auditor expects a high rate of exceptions, so that customers respond in large numbers to the requests
Management has asked the auditor not to contact customers directly
The auditor has assessed the risk as low and has evidence that relevant controls operate effectively
The balances are large and different from one another, so each needs individual attention
items.rule_line: Negative confirmations are the sole procedure only for low risk, many small homogeneous items, and a very low expected exception rate.

why.A: The condition is a very low expected exception rate, not a high one.
why.B: A management request not to confirm is a refusal scenario, not a condition permitting negative confirmations.
why.C: Correct. Negative confirmations alone are acceptable only when risk is low with supporting controls evidence, the population is many small homogeneous items, a very low exception rate is expected, and recipients will not disregard the requests.
why.D: The condition is a large number of small, homogeneous balances.

guide.ask: Under what circumstances is negative confirmation alone acceptable?
guide.reveal: Low assessed risk with supporting control evidence, many small similar items, very few expected exceptions and recipients who will respond.

guide.ask: Which listed condition is one of them?
guide.reveal: Low risk with evidence that relevant controls work.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.3]
items.topic: Management's refusal to allow confirmation
items.task: Perform external confirmations.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Management of Redfield Cement, a nonissuer, asks the auditor not to confirm a $2.4 million receivable with the customer, saying the customer is in a dispute with the company. What should the auditor do?
options: Comply with the request and rely on management's written representation about the balance owed by the customer as evidence
Send the confirmation anyway, using a customer contact provided by the company's sales staff
Inquire about the reasons, evaluate fraud risk implications, and perform alternative procedures to obtain evidence
Withdraw from the engagement immediately
items.rule_line: If management refuses to allow confirmation, inquire, evaluate fraud risk implications, and perform alternative procedures.

why.A: A representation is not a substitute for alternative audit procedures.
why.B: Using a contact supplied by the company would not give the auditor control over the confirmation process.
why.C: Correct. When management refuses, the auditor inquires, evaluates implications for risk including fraud, and performs alternative procedures.
why.D: Withdrawal is not the first step; the auditor evaluates the refusal and considers alternative evidence.

guide.ask: Should the auditor comply with management's request not to confirm?
guide.reveal: Not without examining the reasons.

guide.ask: What steps follow?
guide.reveal: Inquire about the reasons, evaluate implications including fraud risk, and perform alternative procedures.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.3]
items.topic: Nonresponses to positive confirmations
items.task: Analyze external confirmation responses and nonresponses.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Cypress Textiles, a nonissuer, sent positive confirmations to 60 customers. Twelve did not respond after a second request. The auditor has determined that a written response is not necessary to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence. What should the auditor do for each nonresponse?
options: Send negative confirmations to the same customers as a substitute
Perform alternative procedures, such as examining subsequent cash receipts and shipping documents
Treat the nonresponse as confirmation that the recorded balance is correct, because silence implies agreement
Treat each nonresponse as a misstatement and project the total to the population
items.rule_line: Perform alternative procedures for each nonresponse to a positive confirmation request.

why.A: Negative confirmations provide less persuasive evidence and would not substitute for alternative procedures.
why.B: Correct. For each nonresponse the auditor performs alternative procedures to obtain relevant and reliable evidence.
why.C: Silence in response to a positive confirmation is not evidence that the balance is correct.
why.D: A nonresponse is not by itself a misstatement; if a written response were essential, a different treatment would apply.

guide.ask: What does a nonresponse mean to a positive confirmation?
guide.reveal: Nothing about the balance; silence is not agreement.

guide.ask: What must be done for each one?
guide.reveal: Alternative procedures, such as examining subsequent cash receipts and shipping documents.

items.group_name: Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
items.blueprint: AUD.III.D Procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence [III.D.3]
items.topic: Doubts about a confirmation response
items.task: Analyze external confirmation responses, including reliability.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Merrimack Steel, a nonissuer, receives a customer confirmation reply by email from a generic address, not from the confirming party's known domain, and the reply agrees with the recorded balance exactly. The auditor has doubts about its reliability. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Get further evidence, such as calling the customer at an independently verified number
Accept the reply as reliable, because it agrees with the recorded balance and came back promptly
Ask the sales manager to confirm that the customer sent the reply, and file the manager's confirmation
Treat the reply as an exception and propose an adjustment for the full amount of the customer's balance
items.rule_line: Resolve doubts about the reliability of confirmation responses with further evidence.

why.A: Correct. When factors give rise to doubt about reliability, the auditor obtains further evidence to resolve it and considers implications for risk if the response is unreliable.
why.B: Agreement with the recorded balance does not make an unverified response reliable.
why.C: Asking company staff to authenticate the response does not provide independent evidence.
why.D: Doubt about reliability is not the same as an exception, and no misstatement has been shown.

guide.ask: What raises doubt about this reply?
guide.reveal: A generic email address instead of the customer's known domain.

guide.ask: What is the fitting response?
guide.reveal: Obtain further evidence, such as calling the customer at an independently verified number.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.1]
items.topic: Approaches for responding to risks in accounting estimates
items.task: Respond to risks of material misstatement relating to accounting estimates.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Lakemont Insurance, a nonissuer, is responding to assessed risks of material misstatement for an accounting estimate. Which set of approaches may the auditor use?
options: Test only the arithmetical accuracy of management's calculation
Rely on the prior year's audit conclusion if the estimation method has not changed
Request a representation that the estimate is reasonable and limit procedures to the representation
Use events up to the report date, test how management made the estimate, or develop an auditor's range
items.rule_line: Responses to estimate risks: events to the report date, testing management's process, or an auditor's estimate or range.

why.A: Arithmetical accuracy alone does not address methods, assumptions or data.
why.B: Prior-year conclusions do not establish that the current-year estimate is free from misstatement.
why.C: A representation is not sufficient evidence when the risk is assessed, and does not respond to the risk.
why.D: Correct. The further audit procedures for estimates include one or more of these three approaches.

guide.ask: Which approaches are available for responding to risks in an estimate?
guide.reveal: Events up to the report date, testing how management made the estimate, or developing an auditor's range.

guide.ask: Is checking only arithmetic or obtaining a representation enough?
guide.reveal: No, neither provides sufficient evidence alone.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.1]
items.topic: Misstatement when management's estimate is outside the auditor's range
items.task: Evaluate management's accounting estimates against an auditor's range.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Management of Pelham Bank, a nonissuer, records a loan loss allowance of $4,600,000. The auditor develops a range of $3,400,000 to $4,200,000, with each amount in the range supported by sufficient appropriate evidence. What is the misstatement?
items.rule_line: If management's estimate is outside the auditor's range, the misstatement is measured to the nearest end of the range.

why.A: The estimate is outside the range, so a misstatement exists.
why.B: Correct. When management's estimate is outside the auditor's range, the misstatement is the difference between the estimate and the nearest point of the range: $4,600,000 - $4,200,000.
why.C: This measures the difference from the midpoint of the range ($3,800,000), which is not the required measure.
why.D: This measures the difference from the low end of the range, the point farthest from management's estimate.

steps: Management estimate 4,600,000 is above the range 3,400,000 to 4,200,000

guide.ask: Where is management's estimate relative to the range?
guide.reveal: Above it: $4,600,000 versus a range of $3,400,000 to $4,200,000.

guide.ask: How is the misstatement measured?
guide.reveal: From the nearest end of the range: $4,600,000 - $4,200,000 = $400,000.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.1]
items.topic: Using a management's specialist
items.task: Respond to risks relating to accounting estimates that use a management's specialist.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Quarry Hill Foods, a nonissuer, plans to use pension obligation figures prepared by an actuary that management engaged. What must the auditor do to the extent necessary, given the significance of the specialist's work?
options: Obtain a written representation from management that the actuary is qualified and that the figures are accurate
Evaluate the specialist's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and the appropriateness of the work
Refer to the actuary in the auditor's report to make clear that the figures came from an outside specialist
Accept the figures because the actuary is independent of the auditor's firm and holds a professional credential
items.rule_line: Evaluate a management's specialist's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and the appropriateness of the work.

why.A: A representation does not replace the auditor's own evaluation.
why.B: Correct. The auditor evaluates the management's specialist's competence, capabilities and objectivity, understands the work, and evaluates its appropriateness.
why.C: The auditor does not refer to a specialist in an unmodified report.
why.D: Independence from the auditor's firm is not the test; the specialist is engaged by management and the auditor must evaluate objectivity.

guide.ask: Whose work is the actuary's, and what is the auditor expected to do with it?
guide.reveal: Management's specialist; the auditor evaluates it.

guide.ask: What is evaluated?
guide.reveal: The specialist's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and whether the work is appropriate.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.2]
items.topic: Evidence for securities held by a custodian
items.task: Obtain evidence about investments in securities.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Sable Holdings, a nonissuer, has $6.2 million of marketable securities held by a broker on its behalf. Which evidence about existence is most reliable?
options: The auditor's recomputation of unrealized gains using year-end quoted prices
The broker's monthly statement supplied by the treasurer
Minutes of the investment committee approving the purchases
A confirmation the auditor receives directly from the broker
items.rule_line: External confirmation from the custodian is the most reliable evidence of existence for securities.

why.A: Recomputing gains tests valuation, not existence.
why.B: A statement supplied by the client's treasurer is obtained indirectly and is less reliable than a direct confirmation.
why.C: Approval of purchases does not show that the securities are still held.
why.D: Correct. Confirmation obtained directly from the external custodian is the most reliable evidence of existence.

guide.ask: Where do the securities sit and who is the custodian?
guide.reveal: With a broker, an external party.

guide.ask: Which evidence is most reliable for existence?
guide.reveal: A confirmation received directly from the broker, not one supplied by the company.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.2]
items.topic: Investment valued on unaudited investee results
items.task: Obtain evidence about investments in securities.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Halcyon Corp., a nonissuer, carries a 12% investment in a privately held company at an amount based on the investee's financial results. The investee's financial statements are unaudited, and the investment is material. What should the auditor do?
options: Accept management's valuation, because a minority investment does not require the auditor to obtain evidence about the investee's results
Read the unaudited statements and accept them if they are signed by the investee's chief executive officer and chief financial officer
Apply, or have another auditor apply, appropriate procedures to the investee's statements, and consider the opinion if evidence is lacking
Modify the opinion at once, without performing any further procedures on the investee's financial results or asking management for support
items.rule_line: Obtain evidence about an investee's financial results, including procedures on unaudited statements, before concluding on opinion effects.

why.A: The valuation is based on the investee's results, so evidence about those results is needed regardless of ownership percentage.
why.B: Signature by the investee's chief executive does not provide audit evidence about the investee's results.
why.C: Correct. When the investee is unaudited, the auditor applies procedures to its statements or arranges for another auditor to, and modifies the opinion if unable to get sufficient evidence.
why.D: The auditor first tries to obtain evidence; modification follows only if the auditor cannot.

guide.ask: Is the investee audited?
guide.reveal: No, and the investment is material.

guide.ask: What must the auditor do?
guide.reveal: Apply procedures to the investee's statements or have another auditor do so, and consider the opinion if evidence is lacking.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.3]
items.topic: Inventory count not attended for unforeseen reasons
items.task: Obtain evidence about inventory.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Inventory is material to Keystone Hardware, a nonissuer. Severe weather closes the warehouse on the count date, and the auditor cannot attend the count. What should the auditor do?
options: Make or observe some counts on an alternative date and test the intervening transactions
Disclaim an opinion immediately, because attendance at the count is mandatory in all circumstances
Rely on the perpetual inventory records and obtain a management representation about quantities
Ask management to recount the inventory and rely on its results alone
items.rule_line: If unable to attend a count for unforeseen reasons, make or observe counts on another date and test intervening transactions.

why.A: Correct. When attendance is prevented by unforeseen circumstances, the auditor makes or observes some counts on an alternative date and tests intervening transactions.
why.B: Alternative procedures come first; a modified opinion applies only if sufficient evidence cannot be obtained.
why.C: Records and representations do not provide evidence of existence and condition of the inventory.
why.D: Management's recount without the auditor's observation does not give the auditor direct evidence.

guide.ask: Can the auditor simply skip inventory counting?
guide.reveal: No; if attendance is prevented, alternatives exist.

guide.ask: What are they?
guide.reveal: Make or observe some counts on an alternative date and test the intervening transactions.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.3]
items.topic: Test counts during inventory observation
items.task: Obtain evidence about inventory through observation and test counts.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: While observing the physical inventory of Tidewater Lumber, a nonissuer, the auditor wants to test both the existence and the completeness of the count records. Which test counts are most appropriate?
options: Select items from the count sheets only and locate them in the warehouse, testing existence but not completeness
Select items in the warehouse only, and trace them to the perpetual records
Trace items from the count sheets to the warehouse, and items from the warehouse to the count sheets
Select items from the perpetual records and trace them to the count sheets
items.rule_line: Test counts from records to floor test existence; floor to records test completeness.

why.A: This tests existence only and would not detect items on the floor that were omitted from the count.
why.B: This ignores the count sheets, which are the record of what was counted.
why.C: Correct. Tracing from records to the floor tests existence, and tracing from the floor to the records tests completeness, so both directions are needed.
why.D: The perpetual records are not the count records, and this does not test the physical inventory itself.

guide.ask: Which direction of selection tests whether recorded items really exist?
guide.reveal: Starting from the records and going out to the physical items.

guide.ask: Which direction tests whether all existing items were recorded?
guide.reveal: Starting from the physical items and going to the records, so both directions are needed.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.3]
items.topic: Inventory held in a public warehouse
items.task: Obtain evidence about inventory held by third parties.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Mosaic Foods, an issuer, keeps 30% of its inventory in a public warehouse, which is a significant proportion of its assets. Which procedures are appropriate under PCAOB standards?
options: Rely on the warehouse receipts held by the company, because they evidence title to the goods stored there
Confirm directly in writing with the warehouse and apply further procedures, such as observing counts
Obtain a management representation about quantities held, since the warehouse is independent
Perform no procedures, because inventory held by a third party is outside the scope of the audit
items.rule_line: For inventory at public warehouses, confirm with the custodian and apply additional procedures if significant.

why.A: Company-held receipts do not give the auditor direct evidence that the goods are on hand.
why.B: Correct. The auditor ordinarily obtains direct written confirmation from the custodian and, for significant amounts, applies further procedures.
why.C: A representation does not substitute for evidence from the custodian.
why.D: Inventory held by third parties is part of the company's assets and must be audited.

guide.ask: Where is 30% of the inventory held?
guide.reveal: In a third-party public warehouse.

guide.ask: What does PCAOB call for with significant amounts?
guide.reveal: Direct written confirmation with the custodian plus further procedures such as observing counts.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.4]
items.topic: Inquiry of legal counsel
items.task: Obtain evidence about litigation, claims and assessments.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Bristow Tools, a nonissuer, has identified pending litigation that may give rise to a risk of material misstatement. Which is required?
options: Rely on management's description of the litigation and its evaluation, since contact with counsel is optional
Ask legal counsel to respond about all matters of any size, however small
Have management send the inquiry to its lawyer and forward the response to the auditor
Send counsel a letter of inquiry, prepared by management, and seek a direct response from external counsel
items.rule_line: Seek direct communication with external legal counsel by an inquiry letter prepared by management and sent by the auditor.

why.A: Direct communication with counsel is required unless procedures indicate no litigation exists.
why.B: The inquiry covers matters that management considers material, not every matter of any size.
why.C: The auditor must send the letter and receive the response directly to keep control over the process.
why.D: Correct. The auditor seeks direct communication with external counsel through a letter prepared by management and sent by the auditor.

guide.ask: Which party should the auditor contact for litigation?
guide.reveal: External counsel, directly.

guide.ask: Who prepares and who sends the letter?
guide.reveal: Management prepares it and the auditor sends it.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.4]
items.topic: Management refuses to allow contact with counsel
items.task: Obtain evidence about litigation, claims and assessments.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Management of Fairview Homes, a nonissuer, refuses to allow the auditor to communicate with the external lawyer handling a significant lawsuit. Management offers the in-house counsel's written summary instead. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The auditor should modify the opinion, because management refused permission to communicate with external legal counsel
The auditor should modify the opinion only if the in-house counsel's summary is inconsistent with the financial statements
The auditor should rely on management's written assessment of the lawsuit and consider only the adequacy of disclosure
The in-house counsel's summary is an acceptable substitute, so no modification is needed
items.rule_line: Management's refusal to permit communication with external counsel requires a modified opinion.

why.A: Correct. If management refuses permission to communicate with external counsel, the auditor modifies the opinion.
why.B: The refusal by itself requires the modification, regardless of what the summary says.
why.C: Management's own assessment does not replace evidence from external counsel.
why.D: Evidence from in-house counsel is not a substitute for direct communication with external counsel.

guide.ask: Is in-house counsel's summary a substitute for external counsel?
guide.reveal: No, it does not replace direct communication.

guide.ask: What does a refusal to allow contact require?
guide.reveal: Modifying the opinion.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.4]
items.topic: Lawyer's inability to estimate an outcome
items.task: Obtain evidence about litigation, claims and assessments.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In an audit of an issuer, the client's lawyer responds to the inquiry letter that the outcome of a pending lawsuit cannot be estimated because of inherent uncertainties, and the lawyer otherwise responds fully. How should the auditor view this?
options: As a reason to require the lawyer to provide an estimate before the report can be issued
As a limitation on the scope of the audit that precludes an unqualified opinion, the same as a refusal to respond
As an uncertainty about a future outcome affecting the statements, whose effect on the report the auditor considers
As evidence that the lawsuit is not likely to result in an unfavorable outcome
items.rule_line: A lawyer's inability to estimate the outcome is an uncertainty, not a scope limitation; a refusal to respond is a scope limitation.

why.A: Lawyers may not be able to form a conclusion, and the auditor cannot require an estimate.
why.B: A lawyer's refusal to furnish information is a scope limitation; an inability to estimate is different.
why.C: Correct. A lawyer's inability to estimate due to inherent uncertainty is treated as an uncertainty affecting the statements, not a scope limitation.
why.D: The response gives no assurance about the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome.

guide.ask: What does a lawyer's inability to estimate because of inherent uncertainty signal?
guide.reveal: A genuine uncertainty about the future outcome, not a refusal to answer.

guide.ask: How does the auditor treat it?
guide.reveal: As an uncertainty affecting the statements whose effect on the report is considered, not as a scope limitation.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.5]
items.topic: Period for the going concern evaluation of a nonissuer
items.task: Identify factors that raise substantial doubt about an entity's ability to continue as a going concern.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: For which period does the auditor of a nonissuer evaluate whether substantial doubt exists about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern under AICPA standards?
options: The period the framework requires or, if none, one year after issuance or availability of the statements
Only through the date of the auditor's report
Six months after the date of the auditor's report, regardless of the framework's requirements
Twelve months from the balance sheet date only, whatever period the financial reporting framework requires
items.rule_line: AICPA reasonable period: as the framework requires, otherwise one year after the financial statements are issued or available to be issued.

why.A: Correct. A reasonable period is the period the framework requires or, if none, one year after the financial statements are issued or available to be issued.
why.B: The evaluation looks forward beyond the report date, not only through it.
why.C: There is no six-month period in the standard.
why.D: The default measurement date is the issuance (or availability) date, not the balance sheet date.

cite.ref: 570.12 and definition of reasonable period of time

guide.ask: What period does the AICPA standard use for going concern?
guide.reveal: The period the framework requires, or if none, one year after issuance or availability.

guide.ask: Is it limited to the report date or six months?
guide.reveal: No.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.5]
items.topic: Period for the going concern evaluation of an issuer
items.task: Identify factors that raise substantial doubt about an entity's ability to continue as a going concern.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Under PCAOB standards, over what period does the auditor of an issuer evaluate whether there is substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern?
options: Two years after the date of the financial statements being audited by the firm
One year after the date the financial statements are issued, as under the AICPA standard for nonissuers
Only through the date of the auditor's report
A reasonable period not exceeding one year beyond the date of the financial statements
items.rule_line: PCAOB: a reasonable period not to exceed one year beyond the balance sheet date.

why.A: No two-year evaluation period exists.
why.B: The one-year-after-issuance period is from the AICPA standard, not the PCAOB standard.
why.C: The evaluation looks beyond the report date, not only through it.
why.D: Correct. PCAOB standards use a period not to exceed one year beyond the date of the financial statements being audited.

guide.ask: What does the PCAOB standard use for the evaluation period?
guide.reveal: A reasonable period not to exceed one year beyond the statements' date.

guide.ask: How does that differ from the AICPA standard?
guide.reveal: Its reference point is the date of the statements audited, not issuance.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.5]
items.topic: Support from an owner-manager in a going concern evaluation
items.task: Evaluate management's plans and conclude on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: The auditor of Harborview Marine, a nonissuer, finds substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern. Management's plan depends on $1.5 million in funding from the principal owner. The owner gives verbal assurances to the auditor but declines to provide anything in writing. What is the appropriate conclusion?
options: Verbal assurance from the owner is sufficient, because the owner has direct knowledge of the owner's own intent and means
The plans are insufficient to alleviate substantial doubt, because written evidence of the owner's intent is missing
Substantial doubt is alleviated if the owner's financial statements show the ability to provide the funds
A management representation about the owner's intent is adequate support for the plan
items.rule_line: Written evidence of a supporting party's intent to provide funds is required before its support can alleviate substantial doubt.

why.A: Written evidence of intent is required, and oral assurances do not meet the requirement.
why.B: Correct. Failure to obtain written evidence of the supporting party's intent means the plans are insufficient to alleviate substantial doubt.
why.C: Ability to provide funds is not enough; the intent to do so must also be evidenced in writing.
why.D: A management representation does not substitute for the owner's written evidence of intent.

guide.ask: What evidence of the owner's intent is missing?
guide.reveal: Anything in writing, only verbal assurances.

guide.ask: What follows for management's plan?
guide.reveal: It is insufficient to alleviate substantial doubt.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.6]
items.topic: Scope of compliance testing in a single audit
items.task: Test transactions related to federal awards during a single audit.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In a single audit of Fairhaven School District, what must the auditor determine about compliance for each major program?
options: Whether the auditee complied with all federal requirements for every federal program, major or not
Whether the auditee complied only with the requirements the auditee itself considers significant
Compliance with requirements that may have a direct and material effect on each major program
Whether the auditee's financial statements comply with the compliance supplement
items.rule_line: Test compliance with requirements that may have a direct and material effect on each major program.

why.A: Compliance testing is directed at major programs, not every program.
why.B: The auditor, not the auditee, determines which requirements to test.
why.C: Correct. The auditor determines compliance with requirements that may have a direct and material effect on each major program, using the compliance supplement.
why.D: The financial statements are audited under GAAP; the compliance supplement addresses program requirements.

guide.ask: Which compliance requirements does the auditor test for each major program?
guide.reveal: Those that could have a direct and material effect on that program.

guide.ask: Which document guides this?
guide.reveal: The compliance supplement.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.6]
items.topic: Severity of control deficiencies over major programs
items.task: Test transactions related to federal awards and evaluate deficiencies during a single audit.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In a single audit of Cedar County, the auditor finds a deficiency in controls over eligibility for a major program. In relation to what does the auditor determine whether it is a significant deficiency or material weakness for reporting an audit finding?
options: Total federal awards expended by the county
Materiality for the county's financial statements as a whole, as used in the financial statement audit
The county's overall system of internal control across all departments
A type of compliance requirement for the major program identified in the compliance supplement
items.rule_line: Deficiency severity in a single audit is judged in relation to a type of compliance requirement for a major program.

why.A: Total awards expended is used to set Type A thresholds, not to judge severity of deficiencies.
why.B: The basis is the compliance requirement for the major program, not financial statement materiality.
why.C: The evaluation is for controls over major programs, not the entire system.
why.D: Correct. For audit findings, severity is determined in relation to a type of compliance requirement for a major program.

guide.ask: For audit findings, what is severity measured against?
guide.reveal: Not financial statement materiality or total awards.

guide.ask: Against what, then?
guide.reveal: A type of compliance requirement for the major program.

items.group_name: Specific matters that require special consideration
items.blueprint: AUD.III.E Specific matters that require special consideration [III.E.6]
items.topic: Reporting questioned costs in a single audit
items.task: Test transactions related to federal awards and report questioned costs.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In testing allowable costs for a major program at Dover Housing Authority, the auditor identifies known questioned costs of $12,000 and projects likely questioned costs of $31,000 for that type of compliance requirement. What must the auditor do?
options: Report a finding with known questioned costs of $12,000, because likely costs exceed $25,000
Report a finding only if both known and likely questioned costs exceed $25,000
Report a finding that states known questioned costs of $31,000 for the compliance requirement
Report no finding, because the known questioned costs are below the $25,000 reporting threshold
items.rule_line: Report a finding when known or likely questioned costs exceed $25,000 for a compliance requirement of a major program.

why.A: Correct. A finding is required when either known or likely questioned costs exceed $25,000 for a type of compliance requirement for a major program, and it reports the known costs.
why.B: Either known or likely questioned costs above $25,000 are sufficient.
why.C: The finding reports known questioned costs; the likely amount is a projection and is not reported as known.
why.D: The $25,000 test applies to either known or likely questioned costs, so likely costs of $31,000 trigger a finding.

guide.ask: What is the questioned cost reporting threshold?
guide.reveal: $25,000 for a type of compliance requirement.

guide.ask: Which amounts exceed it, and what is reported?
guide.reveal: Likely $31,000 exceeds it while known $12,000 does not; either triggers a finding, reporting the known amount.

items.group_name: Misstatements and internal control deficiencies
items.blueprint: AUD.III.F Misstatements and internal control deficiencies [III.F]
items.topic: Clearly trivial misstatements
items.task: Prepare a summary of misstatements and determine the effect on the financial statements.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which statement about misstatements that are clearly trivial is correct under AICPA standards?
options: When it is uncertain whether an item is clearly trivial, it is treated as clearly trivial
Clearly trivial is not another way to say not material; such items are of a much smaller magnitude
Clearly trivial means any misstatement below materiality for the financial statements as a whole
Clearly trivial misstatements must be accumulated and communicated the same way as all other misstatements
items.rule_line: Clearly trivial misstatements are far smaller than materiality; when uncertain, treat the item as not clearly trivial.

why.A: When there is uncertainty, the item is considered not clearly trivial.
why.B: Correct. Clearly trivial is a much smaller order of magnitude than materiality, and it is not just a synonym for not material.
why.C: Below-materiality misstatements are not automatically clearly trivial and must still be accumulated.
why.D: The auditor accumulates misstatements other than those that are clearly trivial.

guide.ask: Is clearly trivial the same as not material?
guide.reveal: No; it is a much smaller order of magnitude.

guide.ask: If unsure whether an item is clearly trivial, how is it treated?
guide.reveal: As not clearly trivial.

items.group_name: Misstatements and internal control deficiencies
items.blueprint: AUD.III.F Misstatements and internal control deficiencies [III.F]
items.topic: Aggregating uncorrected misstatements
items.task: Prepare a summary of misstatements and determine their effect on the statements and on the nature, timing and extent of procedures.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Materiality for the audit of Ridgeway Steel, a nonissuer, is $200,000. Uncorrected misstatements that each overstate pretax income are a $45,000 factual cutoff error, a $70,000 judgmental difference in the allowance, and $55,000 projected from a receivables sample. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The $170,000 aggregate approaches materiality, so consider revising the plan and request correction
The projected $55,000 should be excluded, because a projected amount is an estimate and not a misstatement
The financial statements are materially misstated, because the aggregate exceeds performance materiality of $150,000
The $170,000 aggregate is below materiality, so no further action is required
items.rule_line: When aggregated misstatements approach materiality, reconsider the audit strategy and plan and request correction.

why.A: Correct. The total is $45,000 + $70,000 + $55,000 = $170,000, which is 85% of materiality. The auditor considers revising the plan and requests correction.
why.B: Projected misstatements are the auditor's best estimate and are evaluated with the others.
why.C: The comparison for material misstatement is with materiality, not performance materiality.
why.D: When the aggregate approaches materiality, the auditor must consider whether the strategy and plan need revision, and being below materiality does not end the analysis.

guide.ask: What is the total of the uncorrected misstatements, including the projected amount?
How does it compare with materiality?
guide.reveal: 85% of $200,000, so consider revising the plan and request correction.

items.group_name: Misstatements and internal control deficiencies
items.blueprint: AUD.III.F Misstatements and internal control deficiencies [III.F]
items.topic: Definition of a significant deficiency
items.task: Determine the effect of internal control deficiencies on the audit.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which describes a significant deficiency in internal control under AICPA standards?
options: Any control failure that causes a misstatement below the level of clearly trivial
A deficiency less severe than a material weakness yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance
A deficiency that results in a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis
A deficiency in an application control that management has already remediated before year-end
items.rule_line: A significant deficiency is less severe than a material weakness but merits the attention of those charged with governance.

why.A: Size of a resulting misstatement is not the definition, and clearly trivial amounts are not the test.
why.B: Correct. This is the definition of a significant deficiency.
why.C: That describes a material weakness, which is more severe.
why.D: Remediation does not change the classification; remediated significant deficiencies are still communicated.

guide.ask: What distinguishes a significant deficiency from a material weakness?
guide.reveal: It is less severe than a material weakness.

guide.ask: Yet what is required of it?
guide.reveal: Attention by those charged with governance.

items.group_name: Misstatements and internal control deficiencies
items.blueprint: AUD.III.F Misstatements and internal control deficiencies [III.F]
items.topic: Indicators of a material weakness in an issuer audit
items.task: Evaluate the severity of internal control deficiencies.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In an integrated audit of an issuer, which finding is an indicator of a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting?
options: A restatement of previously issued financial statements to reflect a change in accounting principle
Auditor identification of an immaterial misstatement the controls would have detected
Identification of fraud, whether or not material, on the part of senior management
A single deficiency in a control over a low-risk account that has an effective compensating control
items.rule_line: Material weakness indicators include senior management fraud, restatements for errors, and ineffective audit committee oversight.

why.A: The indicator is a restatement to correct a material misstatement, not one for a change in principle.
why.B: The indicator is a material misstatement that the controls would not have detected, not an immaterial one that they would have.
why.C: Correct. Fraud by senior management, whether or not material, is an indicator of a material weakness.
why.D: A deficiency with an effective compensating control on a low-risk account is unlikely to be a material weakness.

guide.ask: Which finding is an indicator of a material weakness in an integrated audit?
guide.reveal: Ones like restatement to correct errors, ineffective audit committee oversight, or fraud by senior management.

guide.ask: Which choice is on that list?
guide.reveal: Fraud by senior management, whether or not material; a change in accounting principle is not an error correction.

items.group_name: Written representations
items.blueprint: AUD.III.G Written representations [III.G]
items.topic: Required management representations
items.task: Obtain written representations from management.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which representation must an auditor of a nonissuer request from management?
options: That the audit was conducted in accordance with GAAS and that the evidence obtained was sufficient for the opinion
That management will not dispute the auditor's opinion when it is issued
That management has no obligation to pay the auditor's fee if the opinion is modified
That management provided all relevant information and access, and that all transactions have been recorded
items.rule_line: Required representations cover management's responsibilities, information provided, and completeness of transactions.

why.A: Sufficiency of evidence is the auditor's own conclusion, not a representation from management.
why.B: Management cannot be asked to waive the right to disagree with the opinion.
why.C: Fee arrangements are terms of the engagement, not required representations.
why.D: Correct. Management must represent that it provided all relevant information and access, and that all transactions were recorded.

guide.ask: Which representations are required from management?
guide.reveal: That it provided all relevant information and access and that all transactions are recorded.

guide.ask: Are representations about the auditor's work or fee required?
guide.reveal: No, those are not management's to make.

items.group_name: Written representations
items.blueprint: AUD.III.G Written representations [III.G]
items.topic: Management refuses to provide required representations
items.task: Evaluate management's refusal to provide written representations.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Management of Silverline Foods, a nonissuer, refuses to sign the representation that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation and fair presentation of the financial statements and for internal control. What should the auditor do?
options: Disclaim an opinion on the financial statements or withdraw from the engagement
Perform additional substantive procedures to replace the representation
Accept a letter from management's attorney describing the responsibilities instead
Issue a qualified opinion with a scope limitation paragraph
items.rule_line: If management will not give the representations about its responsibilities, disclaim an opinion or withdraw.

why.A: Correct. If management does not provide the required representations about its responsibilities, the auditor disclaims an opinion or withdraws.
why.B: Other audit evidence cannot replace these representations.
why.C: An attorney's letter is not a written representation from management about its own responsibilities.
why.D: The standard specifies a disclaimer or withdrawal, not a qualified opinion.

guide.ask: Can other procedures replace a refused representation about responsibilities?
guide.reveal: No.

guide.ask: What does the auditor do?
guide.reveal: Disclaim an opinion or withdraw.

items.group_name: Written representations
items.blueprint: AUD.III.G Written representations [III.G]
items.topic: Signing and dating the representation letter for an issuer
items.task: Obtain written representations from management.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: In the audit of Argent Semiconductor, an issuer, which is appropriate for the management representation letter under PCAOB standards?
options: Signed by the controller and dated as of the start of fieldwork
Signed by senior management, normally the CEO and CFO, and dated as of the date of the auditor's report
Signed by the CFO only and dated the day the financial statements are approved by the board
Signed by the audit committee chair only and dated as of the balance sheet date of the statements audited
items.rule_line: Issuer representation letters are signed by senior management (normally CEO and CFO) and dated as of the auditor's report.

why.A: The controller alone is not the normally required signer, and the date must be the report date, not fieldwork start.
why.B: Correct. The letter is signed by those with overall responsibility, normally the CEO and CFO, and is made as of the date of the auditor's report.
why.C: The date must be the auditor's report date, and the letter normally includes the CEO as well as the CFO.
why.D: Representations come from management, not the audit committee chair, and are dated as of the report date.

guide.ask: Who signs the representation letter for an issuer?
guide.reveal: Senior management with overall responsibility, normally the CEO and CFO.

guide.ask: As of what date?
guide.reveal: The date of the auditor's report.

items.group_name: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
items.blueprint: AUD.III.H Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts [III.H]
items.topic: Recognized versus nonrecognized subsequent events
items.task: Identify subsequent events and the impact on the financial statements and disclosures.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Dulcet Retail's financial statements are for the year ended December 31, 2025, and the auditor's report will be dated February 20, 2026. On January 25, 2026, its largest customer files for bankruptcy, and the receivable at year-end had been deteriorating during 2025. How should the event be treated?
options: As a matter outside the audit, because it occurred after the balance sheet date
As an event requiring adjustment only if the bankruptcy had been filed before December 31, 2025
As an event about conditions that arose only after year-end, requiring disclosure without any adjustment
As evidence about conditions existing at year-end, requiring an adjustment to the allowance for credit losses
items.rule_line: Events that give evidence about conditions existing at the balance sheet date require adjustment; others require disclosure only.

why.A: Events through the date of the auditor's report are within the auditor's subsequent events procedures.
why.B: The filing date is not the test; the underlying condition existed before year-end.
why.C: Nonrecognized events relate to conditions that did not exist at the balance sheet date, which is not the situation described.
why.D: Correct. A customer's bankruptcy after year-end that reflects deterioration existing at year-end gives additional evidence about conditions at the balance sheet date and requires adjustment.

verify.note: AS 2801 (PCAOB interim standard) restates the ASC 855 type 1 and type 2 events; classification rests on U.S. GAAP.

guide.ask: Did the customer's condition exist at year-end?
guide.reveal: The receivable had been deteriorating during 2025, so yes.

guide.ask: What treatment follows?
guide.reveal: The bankruptcy provides additional evidence about year-end conditions, so adjust the allowance for credit losses.

items.group_name: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
items.blueprint: AUD.III.H Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts [III.H]
items.topic: Procedures to identify subsequent events
items.task: Identify subsequent events and the impact on the financial statements.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Which procedures should the auditor of a nonissuer perform to identify subsequent events for the period from the balance sheet date to the date of the auditor's report?
options: Reperform the year-end closing procedures for every month in the subsequent period after the balance sheet date
Reconfirm every year-end balance with the original confirming parties as of the report date
Inquire of management and governance, read minutes of later meetings, and read the latest interim statements
Send inquiry letters to all customers and suppliers asking about events since year-end
items.rule_line: Subsequent event procedures: understand management's process, inquire, read later minutes, and read the latest interim statements.

why.A: Reperforming closing procedures does not address events after year-end.
why.B: Reconfirming every balance is not required and would not identify subsequent events.
why.C: Correct. The procedures include inquiring, reading later minutes, and reading the latest interim statements.
why.D: Broad inquiry letters to all customers and suppliers are not among the required procedures.

guide.ask: Which procedures cover the period to the report date?
guide.reveal: Inquiry, reading later minutes and reading the latest interim statements.

guide.ask: Are reperforming closings or mass confirmations expected?
guide.reveal: No, those go beyond the required procedures.

items.group_name: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
items.blueprint: AUD.III.H Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts [III.H]
items.topic: Facts discovered after the report release date
items.task: Identify subsequently discovered facts and their impact on the financial statements and report.
items.task_source: AICPA Uniform CPA Examination Blueprints (Approved Aug. 18, 2025; effective Jan. 2026), AUD; wording paraphrased
items.stem: Two months after the auditor released a report on the 2025 financial statements of Neptune Shipping, a nonissuer, the auditor learns that a warranty reserve was materially understated at the report date. Management does not want to revise the statements, which lenders have already received. What should the auditor do?
options: Discuss it with management and governance and, if not revised, act to prevent reliance on the report
Take no action, because the auditor has no further responsibility once the report has been released
Add a note to the working papers and consider the matter when planning the next year's audit
Withdraw the report by notifying the lenders directly without first informing management or governance
items.rule_line: For facts discovered after release, discuss with management, seek revision, and if needed act to prevent reliance on the report.

why.A: Correct. The auditor discusses the matter, and if management does not revise and take steps to inform third parties, notifies management and governance and takes appropriate action to prevent reliance.
why.B: The auditor has responsibilities for facts that existed at the report date and become known after release.
why.C: Deferring the matter to next year's audit would leave the users relying on the report.
why.D: The auditor first works with management and those charged with governance before seeking to prevent reliance.

guide.ask: Is the auditor's responsibility over once the report is released?
guide.reveal: No, it continues when facts existing at the report date come to light.

guide.ask: What steps follow if management will not revise?
guide.reveal: Discuss with management and governance and, if not revised, act to prevent reliance on the report.
